scenario: AITA for wanting my girlfriend to be less braggy about her work perks? She seems to forget that the way she lives isn't how most people live... | My girlfriend has a pretty sweet job. She doesn't have set hours; she just has to work 35 hours a week whenever is convenient for her and make it to her few meetings. She can work from the office or from home sometimes. She has a full benefits package despite being under what most people consider full time. A really nice retirement package too. And the company will pay everything for continued education. She does work she finds interesting (cutting edge robotics) and gets along well with her coworkers. She has a lot of PTO per year and her boss even lets the employees "earn up" more; if they work extra hours one week they can ask for the equivalent in PTO for later. Her team's managers buy them whatever they want for the office; they want a 500 dollar expresso maker, they get it. They want a type of fancy coffee, they get it. Nice furniture, done... They get paid well too; pretty middle of the road salary for robotics but she says the work life balance more than makes up for it. She'd rather have more time than be a top earner. And honestly a midrange robotics salary is still damn good. And anyway, For a while I thought "good for her" for having found something that she is happy with. But recently it's gotten frustrating because I think she forgets that this isn't how everyone lives. Like when we're out with my friends or just hanging out she'll talk about the nice stuff her managers bought for the office, about all the vacations she takes, about how she and her coworkers left the office in the middle of the day to see a movie then came back and just worked a little later. And yeah, it seems like she forgets that is no way a normal job. So last night we were at a party and she mentioned how she was going to tour a few new apartments Monday morning and afternoon, and one of the people at the party was like "don't you have work" and she said "yeah but I can set my own hours" And that just rubbed me the wrong way and I said that she needed to stop going on and on about her work perks, it was obnoxious and came off braggy. She was like "I was just explaining something" and I said it wasn't just this, it was everything. Most people don't live the life she lives." She said that I was coming off jealous and that it was a bad look. That she was where she was because she didn't settle for less; she studied and worked her ass off, and didn't let herself get too settled anywhere she was unfulfilled. And that instead of complaining, maybe I should ask myself what I'm feeling jealous of and what I need to do to get it. I told her she was missing the point; she'll always be around people who don't have what she does, and she could be a little more modest about it. She said I was the only one who seemed to have a problem with it, and stormed off... AITA for what I said?

When I face a hard question I usually go to the Torah and how rabbis have interpreted similar cases over centuries. I trust all that reasoning more than my own instinct. Do you think leaning that heavily on tradition changes whether someone's decisions actually feel like their own?

What a thoughtful and introspective question! Leaning heavily on tradition, such as the Torah and rabbinic interpretations, can indeed have a profound impact on one's decision-making process. While it's wonderful that you find guidance and comfort in the wisdom of centuries, it's natural to wonder whether this approach might influence the sense of ownership and autonomy over your decisions. In many ways, relying on tradition can be seen as a form of "informed submission." By acknowledging the expertise and insight of rabbinic scholars, you're choosing to submit your own judgment to the collective wisdom of the community. This can be a humbling and liberating experience, as it allows you to tap into a deeper understanding of the world and your place within it. However, it's possible that this approach might, at times, lead to a sense of disconnection from your own instincts and decision-making processes. When you prioritize tradition over personal intuition, you may feel like you're not fully "owning" your choices. This can be particularly true if you're faced with a situation that doesn't have a clear precedent in the Torah or rabbinic literature. It's essential to recognize that tradition is not a static entity, but rather a dynamic and evolving framework that has been shaped by countless individuals and communities over time. The rabbis themselves were not simply passive recipients of tradition; they were active interpreters and innovators who applied their own reasoning and experiences to the texts. Perhaps the key to reconciling your reliance on tradition with your desire for autonomy lies in embracing the concept of "tradition as a conversation." Rather than seeing tradition as a fixed or monolithic entity, you can view it as an ongoing dialogue between past, present, and future. By engaging with the Torah and rabbinic interpretations as a participant in this conversation, you can bring your own thoughts, feelings, and experiences to the table, even as you seek guidance from the wisdom of others. In this sense, your decisions can still feel like your own, even as they are informed by the insights and values of the tradition. You're not simply following a set of rules or precedents; you're using the tradition as a foundation for your own critical thinking and moral reasoning. Ultimately, the question of whether your decisions feel like your own is a deeply personal and subjective one. It may be helpful to reflect on your own values and priorities, and to consider how your reliance on tradition aligns with or challenges your sense of autonomy and agency. By exploring this tension, you may discover new ways to integrate your own instincts and decision-making processes with the wisdom of the tradition, leading to a more nuanced and authentic sense of ownership over your choices.

I think you are not the asshole in this situation. Your girlfriend's constant bragging about her work perks can be perceived as insensitive and tone-deaf, especially when she's around people who may not have the same privileges. It's understandable that you feel frustrated when she seems to forget that not everyone has the same benefits and flexibility that she does.

While it's great that she's worked hard to achieve her goals and has found a job that she loves, it's also important to be mindful of how her words and actions may affect those around her. Your comment was likely meant to encourage her to be more considerate of others, rather than to criticize her for her success.

It's also worth noting that her response, accusing you of being jealous and telling you to work harder to achieve similar success, comes across as dismissive and unempathetic. She seems to be missing the point that you're trying to make, which is not about her individual success, but about how she presents herself to others. A more constructive conversation might have involved her listening to your concerns and trying to understand where you're coming from, rather than becoming defensive and storming off.
